title: Rosa Parks: Agent of Change
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant profile Rosa Parks, from her childhood in Pine Level, Alabama, and her activism with the NAACP in Montgomery, through her December 1, 1955 arrest for refusing to give up her bus seat, the Montgomery Bus Boycott, the Browder v. Gayle case that ended bus segregation, and her later life in Detroit, her honors, and the release of her personal papers. The episode closes with listener mail about tiny things and the Museum of Jurassic Technology.
topics: Rosa Parks papers Library of Congress

segments.title: Opening banter and tour dates
segments.summary: Hosts mention upcoming tour dates, the studio cleanup, and introduce Rosa Parks as a figure whose fuller story has emerged in recent years.

segments.title: Rosa Parks' fuller picture and sources
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how Rosa Parks was often whittled down to a tired, meek seamstress, why the civil rights movement presented her that way, and how her personal papers, donated to the Library of Congress, revealed a committed activist. They recommend a Great Black Heroes article and the Little People, Big Dreams children's book series.

segments.title: Early life in Pine Level and Tuskegee
segments.summary: Parks is born in Tuskegee, Alabama, in 1913 to James and Leona McCauley. She moves to her grandparents' home in Pine Level as a child, where her grandfather, a former enslaved man, taught her to resent white injustice. She attends a segregated school, the Montgomery Industrial School for Girls.

segments.title: Marriage, activism and NAACP work
segments.summary: Parks drops out of school to care for family, marries Raymond Parks at nineteen, and finishes school at his urging. Raymond was a grassroots activist. Parks works as secretary for the Montgomery NAACP for about fourteen years, investigating sexual assaults against Black women, and gains contacts for the coming movement. A job at Maxwell Air Force Base and a Highlander Folk School workshop broaden her experience.

segments.title: Segregation customs on Montgomery buses
segments.summary: Hosts explain that Montgomery bus segregation rested on local ordinance plus unwritten custom: the colored section, moving the sign back, and standing or leaving when white seats ran out. Courts treated breaking the custom as breaking the law.

segments.title: December 1, 1955 arrest
segments.summary: On December 1, 1955, Parks boards the Cleveland Avenue bus after work. Driver James Blake had previously humiliated her about twelve years earlier. When white passengers need seats, Parks refuses to move, and is arrested, booked for disorderly conduct, and bailed out by Clifford Durr and Edgar Nixon. Hosts note Claudette Colvin and Mary Louise Smith were arrested earlier that year.

segments.title: Boycott launch and early demands
segments.summary: Churches and the Women's Political Council distribute handbills calling for a one-day boycott on Monday. The response is far larger than expected. Demands start modest: courtesy, first-come seating, and Black drivers on Black routes. Parks is found guilty and appeals. Martin Luther King Jr. is elected president of the Montgomery Improvement Association, and his home is bombed.

segments.title: Carpools, legal fight and Browder v. Gayle
segments.summary: The MIA runs a carpool of station wagons that carries many riders daily, hurting bus finances. The city sues, and the boycott is challenged under an old Alabama anti-boycott law. King is convicted and fined. Browder v. Gayle, a class action by four women, challenges bus segregation's constitutionality. Attorney Fred Gray keeps Parks' case separate.

segments.title: Supreme Court ruling and end of bus segregation
segments.summary: The federal district court rules two to one that bus segregation is unconstitutional, citing Brown v. Board of Education. The Supreme Court affirms unanimously. The boycott ends after roughly 381 days, and buses are desegregated; Parks sits in the front. The episode links this to Plessy v. Ferguson's overturning and the national spotlight on King.

segments.title: Later life, honors and papers
segments.summary: Parks and Raymond face job losses and move to Virginia and then Detroit. She works for Congressman John Conyers for many years. After Raymond's death in 1977, she founds a scholarship foundation. She is robbed and beaten in her home in 1994. She receives many honors, lies in honor at the Capitol rotunda, and dies in 2005. Her papers, bought by the Howard Buffett Foundation in 2014, show her as a lifelong activist.

segments.title: Listener mail: tiny things
segments.summary: A listener recommends the Museum of Jurassic Technology in Los Angeles, with its Needle exhibit of miniature sculptures and micro mosaics made with butterfly wings. The hosts discuss the museum and tangents about Jack Palance. Sign-off with social media and website info.
